submission.natural_language_explanation: L5H2 is a retrospective phrase-boundary head: at the right edge of an embedded phrase (the phrase's last token, or the first token after it) it leaves the position-0 attention sink and attends to the token that opened that phrase - a preposition, an opening comma, a relative or subordinating marker, a determiner, or the first word of a compound or coordination - so its write is a copy of the opener's value. It peaks (strength 10-22 of the 21.4 max) exactly on those closure tokens, typically the determiner, quantifier, complementizer or phrase-final noun where a mid-sentence PP or parenthetical ends and the host clause resumes ('not until X that Y', 'excluded from X everything', 'saw in the mirror a figure'), stays near its floor (2-5) inside the phrase, at a text's first token and usually on ordinary content words, and its weaker 5-10 firings are the same rule applied to short phrases (compounds, 'and'-coordination, determiner+noun); mean ablation moves next-token probability diffusely, so it marks a boundary rather than preparing a specific upcoming token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Bellwether had always been a harbour town, and it had always been a poor one. The cannery on the eastern quay closed the year before Marta was born, and the fishing fleet shrank a little every season, until only four boats still went out before dawn. The families who owned them argued about moorings at the parish council, and the arguments were reported in the weekly paper with a seriousness that the rest of the county found funny. Tourists came in July and August, bought ice cream, photographed the shuttered ice house, and left. What none of them noticed was how few children there were in the school photographs, and how the same four surnames filled every page of the church register. Marta had left at nineteen and come back at fifty. She came back because her sister had died in March and somebody had to sort through the house on Cooper Street, which had been in the family since the war. The rooms smelled of dust and lavender and something older underneath. In the attic, beneath a sheet of tarpaulin, she found boxes of invoices, a broken concertina, a crate of school exercise books, and a bundle of letters tied with ribbon. She carried the letters down to the kitchen, made tea, and opened the first one under the light of a single bulb. The letters were from a man named Aldous Reed. He had worked the summer boats in 1961 and had written to her mother every week until the fleet moved north for the herring. His handwriting was cramped and careful, and he described the weather, the price of fuel, and the quarrels among the crew with the patience of a man who believed that small things deserved attention. Marta read for three hours without stopping. By the end she understood why her mother had kept the bundle, and why she had never mentioned it. Outside, the tide had turned. A gull screamed above the roof and the town clock struck eleven with its usual cracked note. She carried her tea to the window and watched the lights of a trawler crawl across the bay. The harbour had not changed, she thought; she had. She sat with the bundle for a long time after that, turning the top letter over in her hands and listening to the house settle. The boiler ticked in the cupboard behind the kitchen wall, and somewhere upstairs a window rattled in the wind off the water. She thought about her sister, who had never liked the house and had said so at every Christmas dinner, and about her mother, who had never once explained the letters or apologized for keeping them. None of it was written down anywhere; it existed only in the rooms and in the handwriting of a man who had been dead for twenty years. In the morning she took the letters to the museum on the high street. The curator was a thin woman with round glasses who listened to the whole story without interrupting and then, after turning the pages over twice and checking the postmarks against a ledger, agreed to accept the collection on loan. Marta signed the forms, shook hands, and walked home along the quay. The cannery still stood at the end of the point, rusting quietly, and beyond it the water went on being water.
